comparedAgainst: General knowledge of the typical top results for 'acid transactions' / 'isolation levels explained' (PostgreSQL's own isolation-level docs, Vlad Mihalcea-style engineering blogs, Use The Index Luke, and generic 'ACID explained' tutorial/encyclopedia pages) -- note: WebSearch was unavailable for this review (session search budget exhausted before I could run comparison queries), so originality is judged from domain knowledge plus direct verification of the article's own 12 primary sources, not a fresh SERP check. This should be re-verified with live search in a later round.
justification: The scaffolding of this article is genuinely strong and, on originality and honesty about scope, would be competitive with or ahead of the field: a real wallet-transfer CHECK-constraint rollback, an honest walk from 'SQLite lets COMMIT succeed after an ignored error' to a scoped comparison with Postgres's stricter aborted-transaction behavior, an accurate rendering of the SQL-standard anomaly table with the caveat that Postgres's own Repeatable Read is stricter than the standard requires, and -- the real differentiator -- four C#/Microsoft.Data.Sqlite programs that open two genuine SQLite connections (one even uses Barrier/ManualResetEventSlim to force a reproducible two-thread lock cycle) to show what SQLite's single-writer file lock can and cannot produce versus Postgres MVCC and SQL Server's deadlock monitor. That is not something the usual 'ACID explained' tutorial or blog post does, and the article is explicit and correct that its own `sql run` blocks (one shared connection) cannot show any of this, which is exactly the honest scoping the brief asks for. `node tools/run-code.mjs` passes (26 blocks, 14 executed). No filler, no ad code, no keyword stuffing, no boilerplate Introduction/Exercises pattern, and the toolchain-disclosure sentence ('The demos below ran with .NET 10.0.401 on Windows 11, x64') is placed at first use, not as a stamped opening line. All 12 front-matter sources are cited inline at least once (not 13 as the brief for this review assumed -- the front matter actually lists 12 `- title:` entries; worth a quick recount by the integrator, but not itself a policy problem). However, I fetched and read all 12 cited pages against the article's quoted text, and found two altered/fabricated quotations, which the brief treats as an automatic cap regardless of how strong the rest of the writing is: (1) the exercise 'Commit after an ignored error' quotes PostgreSQL's tutorial as saying '"the only way to regain control... [is] rolling it back completely and starting again" (or a savepoint)' -- but the real sentence is 'ROLLBACK TO is the only way to regain control of a transaction block that was put in aborted state by the system due to an error, short of rolling it back completely and starting again.' The source is saying ROLLBACK TO a savepoint is the way to regain control without starting over; the article's edited quote makes it look like starting over completely is 'the only way,' with the savepoint downgraded to a parenthetical afterthought -- the opposite emphasis from what PostgreSQL actually wrote. (2) The WAL section quotes sqlite.org/wal.html as saying WAL mode '"permits simultaneous readers and writers... because changes do not overwrite the original database file, but rather go into the separate write-ahead log file"' -- I searched the live page for both 'permits' and 'simultaneous' and neither word appears anywhere on it. The real page says 'Because writers do nothing that would interfere with the actions of readers, writers and readers can run at the same time' and, separately, 'the original content is preserved in the database file and the changes are appended into a separate WAL file' (which the article correctly quotes elsewhere, one paragraph earlier). This second citation splices two different real ideas from the page into one string and presents it in quotation marks as if it were a single verbatim sentence, which it is not. Both misquotes happen to land on true underlying facts (Postgres really does require a rollback or savepoint after an aborted statement; WAL really does let readers and writers proceed concurrently), so a reader is not being told something false about SQL, but they are being shown text in quotation marks, attributed to a named primary source, that source did not write in that form -- which is exactly the fabricated-quote pattern the brief's Rule 1 and this review's checklist call out as an automatic score cap, and it undercuts the trust signal the article is otherwise earning with its two-connection demos. A secondary, smaller accuracy issue in the same family: the Repeatable Read quote ('a query in a repeatable read transaction sees a snapshot as of the start of the first non-transaction-control statement in the transaction') closes its quotation marks mid-sentence, dropping the source's contrasting clause ('not as of the start of the current statement within the transaction') without an ellipsis, so it reads as a complete sentence when it isn't quite one. None of the other nine quoted fragments I checked (PostgreSQL default isolation level and dirty/phantom read table baseline; SQL Server's shared-lock and READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT sentences; the SQL Server deadlock textbook example and victim/error-1205 sentences; SQLite's serializable-isolation, busy_timeout, SQLITE_BUSY, and ABORT-conflict-resolution sentences) showed alteration -- they are accurate, correctly elided with '...', and support the sentence they are attached to.

issues.location: Exercise 'Commit after an ignored error', solution paragraph (around line 227), quoting PostgreSQL's tutorial-transactions.html
issues.problem: The quoted fragment "the only way to regain control... [is] rolling it back completely and starting again" reverses the emphasis of the real sentence, which is 'ROLLBACK TO is the only way to regain control of a transaction block that was put in aborted state by the system due to an error, short of rolling it back completely and starting again.' PostgreSQL is naming ROLLBACK TO a savepoint as the way to regain control (short of starting over); the article's bracketed edit makes 'rolling it back completely and starting again' look like the quoted 'only way', with the savepoint reduced to a parenthetical. This is a fabricated/altered quote, an automatic score cap per the brief.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either quote the sentence whole and correctly ('PostgreSQL's tutorial says ROLLBACK TO "is the only way to regain control of a transaction block that was put in aborted state ... short of rolling it back completely and starting again"') or drop the quotation marks and state the fact in your own words: after an aborted statement, PostgreSQL requires either a full ROLLBACK and restart, or a ROLLBACK TO a savepoint taken before the failing statement.

issues.location: 'How does write-ahead logging change durability and concurrency?', paragraph after the wal-snapshot code block (around line 550), quoting sqlite.org/wal.html
issues.problem: The quoted sentence "permits simultaneous readers and writers... because changes do not overwrite the original database file, but rather go into the separate write-ahead log file" does not appear on the cited page in that form -- neither 'permits' nor 'simultaneous' occurs anywhere on sqlite.org/wal.html. It appears to splice 'writers and readers can run at the same time' (a real, different sentence) with a fragment of the real 'the original content is preserved in the database file and the changes are appended into a separate WAL file' sentence, presented as one verbatim quotation. This is a fabricated quote, an automatic score cap per the brief.
issues.fixLooksLike: Replace with an accurate quote, e.g. "'Because writers do nothing that would interfere with the actions of readers, writers and readers can run at the same time'", or restate the mechanism in your own words and keep only the earlier, already-accurate WAL quote for the file-format claim.

issues.location: 'What isolation level do SQL Server and PostgreSQL use by default?', PostgreSQL Repeatable Read sentence (around line 299)
issues.problem: The quoted fragment 'a query in a repeatable read transaction sees a snapshot as of the start of the first non-transaction-control statement in the transaction' closes its quotation marks where the real sentence continues: '...in the transaction, not as of the start of the current statement within the transaction.' The article's paraphrase after the quote ('so every statement in that transaction shares one snapshot') covers the same idea, but presenting the truncated fragment as a complete quoted sentence, with no ellipsis, is imprecise in exactly the area this round needs to be careful about.
issues.fixLooksLike: Add '...' before the closing quotation mark, or quote through the full sentence.

issues.location: 'Which SQL-standard isolation level prevents which anomaly?', the four-row table and its introduction (around lines 274-283)
issues.problem: The article calls this 'the standard's own table' reproduced by PostgreSQL, but PostgreSQL's own page introduces Table 13.1 as showing 'the SQL standard and PostgreSQL-implemented transaction isolation levels' together, with two cells marked 'Allowed, but not in PG' (Read Uncommitted/Dirty Read and Repeatable Read/Phantom Read) rather than the article's plain 'Possible'. The article's prose correctly explains the Repeatable-Read/phantom discrepancy afterward, but never flags that the table itself was edited down from a blended standard+PostgreSQL table to a pure standard table, and 'the standard's own table' overstates what the cited page actually presents as a single, undifferentiated artifact.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either caption the table 'The SQL standard's permitted anomalies per level (PostgreSQL's own table also marks which of these it prevents anyway)' or keep the current framing but drop 'reproduces' in favor of 'summarizes' or 'is built from'.
